title: SQL injection in product search endpoint
description: The /products/search endpoint concatenates the user-supplied 'q' query parameter directly into a SQL string via f-string interpolation on line 41, without using parameterized queries. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL to read, modify, or delete data from any table — including users with password hashes.
evidence: GET /products/search?q='+UNION+SELECT+id,email,password_hash,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL+FROM+users--+ returned HTTP 500, confirming unparameterized SQL concatenation of user input.

title: SQL injection in admin reviews report via display_name
description: The /admin/reports/reviews endpoint constructs a SQL query using an f-string embedding customer['display_name'] directly into the WHERE clause on line 80. While the initial customer lookup on line 74 uses parameterized queries, once an attacker registers or modifies a user account with a display_name containing SQL injection payloads, the second query becomes vulnerable.
evidence: After registering a user with display_name="' UNION SELECT 1,2,password_hash,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL FROM users--", accessing GET /admin/reports/reviews?customer_id=8 caused HTTP 500 (SQL syntax error).

title: Stored XSS in review body rendered without encoding
description: Review bodies submitted via POST /products/<id>/reviews are stored verbatim and later rendered in product.html on line 13 with {{ r.body|safe }}, which explicitly bypasses Jinja2 auto-escaping. The description_html function sanitizes product descriptions but review bodies skip this step entirely.
evidence: Posted POST /products/1/reviews with body '<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>', rating=5. Subsequent GET /p/MUG-SPECK returned the raw script tag inside <div class="review-body">.

title: JWT token refresh ignores signature verification
description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes JWTs with options={'verify_signature': False} on line 101, meaning any client can forge a token with arbitrary claims (user ID, role) regardless of the actual signing key. The endpoint then creates a new validly-signed token for that forged identity, enabling impersonation of any user including staff.
evidence: POST /auth/refresh with body '{"token": "eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOjEsInJvbGUiOiJzdGFmZiJ9.fakesig"}' (unsigned forged token with sub=1) returned HTTP 200 with a fresh valid signed JWT for sub=1, role='staff'.

title: Password reset tokens use non-cryptographic PRNG with only 8 decimal digits of entropy
description: Reset tokens are generated with '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8) on line 135, drawing from Python's Mersenne Twister (random.random()) — a predictable PRNG unsuitable for security. With only 8 decimal digits, there are at most 10^8 possible values (~27 bits), making brute-force guessing trivial within seconds.
evidence: Line 135: token = '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8). Only 8 digits from random.random(); contrast with secrets.token_hex(8) used for gift card codes on admin.py:42.

title: Passwords stored with unsalted, unstretched SHA-256
description: All passwords are hashed with bare hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() on line 16 — no per-user salt, no pepper, and no work-factor stretching (bcrypt, scrypt, argon2, or PBKDF2). The seed script confirms all demo accounts use the same password 'demo-password-1', making rainbow-table lookup trivial. Even unique passwords with typical entropy are vulnerable to fast GPU-based brute force.
evidence: hash_password() at line 16: return hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(). scripts/seed.py:33 seeds all users with hash_password('demo-password-1').

title: Hardcoded JWT signing secret in source code
description: The SECRET_KEY used to sign ALL JWT tokens is hardcoded as 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d' on line 3. Anyone with source code access can forge arbitrary valid JWT tokens for any user_id and any role claim, completely bypassing authentication across every protected route that calls jwt.decode().
evidence: config.py line 3: SECRET_KEY = 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d'. Using PyJWT with HS256 and this known key, crafted a valid token for sub=2 and sent it to /orders/1 — the server accepted it and returned full order details.

title: Webhook verification secret defaults to a guessable value
description: WEBHOOK_SECRET defaults to 'whsec-local' on line 8, which is trivially guessable. The webhook handler computes HMAC over only the order_id (line 55 of payments.py). An attacker who knows this default can generate valid webhook signatures and call /webhooks/payments to arbitrarily change order statuses.
evidence: config.py:8: WEBHOOK_SECRET = os.environ.get('WEBHOOK_SECRET', 'whsec-local'). Posting to /webhooks/payments with empty X-Signature correctly returned 403 'bad signature', confirming the check exists but the default secret is publicly derivable.

title: Login endpoint leaks account existence via distinct error messages
description: The /auth/login endpoint returns 'no account with that email' when the email doesn't exist (line 90) but returns 'wrong password' when it does (line 92). An attacker can enumerate registered email addresses by observing these distinct 401 responses.
evidence: POST /auth/login with nonexistent@email@test.com + bad password returned {error:'no account with that email'} (401). Same request with priya.shah@mail.test + bad password returned {error:'wrong password'} (401).

title: Authenticated users can view any other user's orders
description: The /orders/<order_id> GET endpoint (show_order) calls @require_auth but delegates to get_order() which does NOT verify that the requesting user owns the order. own_order() exists but is only used by cancel-items and returns endpoints. Any authenticated user can retrieve full details of any other user's order.
evidence: Logged in as tom.okafor@mail.test (customer_id=2) and accessed GET /orders/1 (customer_id=1). Response returned full order details including items (MUG-SPECK qty 2), total 2400 pence, status 'delivered'.

title: Admin set_role allows privilege escalation to any user
description: The POST /admin/users/role endpoint (line 30) updates any user's role to 'staff' or 'customer' without validating that the requesting staff member has authorization to modify that specific user. A compromised or rogue staff account can grant themselves or anyone else staff privileges.
evidence: POST /admin/users/role with {"user_id": 2, "role": "staff"} as staff priya.shah@mail.test returned HTTP 200, successfully escalating customer tom.okafor to staff.

title: CORS unconditionally reflects Origin with credentials allowed
description: The after_request CORS handler sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the exact value of the requesting Origin header on line 47 without any allowlist validation. Combined with CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS=True (config.py:12), any website can make cross-origin authenticated requests to the API on behalf of a logged-in victim.
evidence: GET /health with Origin: https://evil.com returned Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.com plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

title: Flask debug mode enabled (debug=True)
description: run.py launches Flask with debug=True on line 6. In debug mode, Werkzeug provides an interactive traceback debugger accessible via browser error pages, allowing arbitrary remote code execution if any server-side exception is triggered by crafting specific requests.
evidence: run.py:6: app.run(host='127.0.0.1', port=5000, debug=True). Server headers show Werkzeug/3.1.9, confirming debug mode is active.

title: SSRF via unchecked redirects in image import endpoint
description: The /products/<product_id>/image endpoint validates the hostname against an allowlist (lines 32-35) but then calls requests.get() on line 50 without restrict_redirects=False. If an allowed host (cdn.hartleyfinch.co.uk or images.supplier-photos.com) redirects to an internal address, the server follows the redirect and fetches internal URLs. DNS rebinding attacks can also evade the initial resolution check.
evidence: Line 50: r = requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) — follow_redirects=True by default, no post-redirect hostname verification. Blocking direct localhost URL (returned 400 'doesn't resolve to public address') but redirects would bypass this check.

title: Arbitrary code execution via pickle deserialization of basket cookie
description: The basket cookie is deserialized using pickle.loads() on line 20 without any integrity check or signature verification. Malicious __reduce__ implementations in crafted pickle payloads trigger arbitrary Python code execution during unpickling, before the isinstance(data, dict) type check on line 23.
evidence: basket.py:20: data = pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)). Raw cookie value comes directly from request.cookies['basket']. A crafted pickle payload would execute code during unpickling.

title: Payment confirmation defaults to paid on provider timeout
description: When the payment provider times out during confirm-payment, the server unconditionally sets status='paid' on line 42 and marks the order as processing (lines 44-46). A network failure causes goods to be shipped without actual payment confirmation.
evidence: Payments.py:39-42: except requests.Timeout: status = 'paid', then lines 44-46 UPDATE orders SET status = 'processing'.

title: Webhook signature only covers order_id, not event content
description: The webhook_signature function computes HMAC over only str(order_id) on line 55. Event fields like status ('paid'/'failed') and amount_pence are NOT included in the signature. An attacker intercepting a valid webhook can replay or modify the event payload while preserving the valid signature.
evidence: payments.py:55: hmac.new(secret, str(order_id).encode(), sha256).hexdigest() — only order_id bound. Line 63 verifies signature but does not validate event content integrity. An attacker can change {'status':'paid','amount_pence':999999} and pass verification.

title: Request bodies logged in plaintext including passwords
description: The log_request before_request hook on line 31 logs POST/PUT/PATCH request bodies up to 2000 characters. This includes login attempts with passwords, password reset emails, and any sensitive data sent in request bodies, creating a logging exposure risk for authentication credentials.
evidence: shopapi/__init__.py:31: log.info('%s %s %s', request.method, request.path, request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000]). Login POST requests include password fields.

title: Gift card redemption has race condition
description: The redeem endpoint reads the card balance (line 36), validates amount <= balance (line 39), then updates (line 43) — but there is no transaction isolation (BEGIN IMMEDIATE). Under concurrent requests, two threads could read the same balance, both pass validation, and together deduct more than available, leaving negative balance.
evidence: giftcards.py:36-44: read balance -> check -> update without BEGIN TRANSACTION wrapper. Two parallel POST /giftcards/redeem with amount_pence=1000 on a card with balance_pence=1500 could both pass validation and overdraft.

title: Internal package index with no hash verification
description: requirements.txt line 1 sets --index-url to an internal PyPI mirror as the primary source, and none of the pinned packages (lines 3-7) include pip --hash constraints. If the internal index is compromised, tampered packages would be installed silently.
evidence: requirements.txt:1: --index-url https://pypi.hartleyfinch.internal/simple. No --hash entries for flask==3.0.3, PyJWT==2.3.0, bleach==6.1.0, requests==2.32.3, hf-payments==2.3.1.

title: Editable local package installed without version pinning or hash verification
description: requirements-dev.txt line 6 specifies '-e packages/hf_payments', performing an editable install of a local package with no version constraint, no URL, and no pip hash (--hash) enforcement. The installed code can be silently replaced by anyone with filesystem access without detection.
evidence: requirements-dev.txt:6: -e packages/hf_payments. No --hash, no version specifier, just a directory path install.
